title: Warehouse Routes
statement: A floor robot starts at the top-left cell of a warehouse grid and must reach the bottom-right cell, moving only one cell right or one cell down at a time. grid is a list of equal-length rows where '.' is open floor and '#' is a shelf the robot cannot enter. Count the different routes, modulo 1000000007. If the start or the destination is a shelf, there are no routes.
constraints: 1 <= grid[i].length <= 100, all rows have equal length

examples.explanation: The shelf in the middle leaves two routes: around the top-right or around the bottom-left.
Right then down, or down then right.

hints.content: Every route into a cell arrives either from the cell above or from the cell to the left.
So routes(r, c) = routes(r - 1, c) + routes(r, c - 1) for an open cell, and 0 for a shelf.
Exploring every route one by one is exponential; count them instead.
Fill a table row by row so both neighbors are ready when you need them.
One row of counts is enough: ways[c] still holds the value from the row above, and ways[c - 1] already holds this row's left neighbor. Apply the modulo after each addition.

testCases.explanation: The shelf in the middle leaves two routes: around the top-right or around the bottom-left.
Right then down, or down then right.
Start and destination are the same open cell: one route.
A blocked start allows no routes.
Shelves in the corners still leave some routes.
Both paths out of the start are blocked.
A blocked destination allows no routes.
An open 10 × 10 grid has C(18, 9) = 48620 routes.
A wide open grid where the count must be taken modulo 1000000007.

solutions.title: Walk every route recursively
solutions.intuition: From each cell, the routes to the destination are the routes going right plus the routes going down.
solutions.approach: walk(r, c) returns 0 off the grid or on a shelf, 1 at the destination, and otherwise walk(r + 1, c) + walk(r, c + 1).
solutions.pseudocode: walk(r, c): if outside or shelf: 0; if destination: 1; return walk(r+1, c) + walk(r, c+1)
commonMistakes: Forgetting to check whether the start itself is a shelf.
Counting the destination cell twice by also recursing out of it.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Recursion mirrors the definition, but the same cell is reached by many routes and recounted every time, so the running time is exponential.

steps.title: Step 1
steps.content: From (0,0) in ['...','.#.','...'], going right leads only around the top-right, which is one route.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Going down leads only around the bottom-left, which is one route. Total 2.

solutions.title: Rolling one-row table
solutions.intuition: The number of routes into a cell depends only on the cell above and the cell to the left.
solutions.approach: ways[0] = 1 if the start is open. For each row and column: a shelf sets ways[c] = 0; otherwise ways[c] += ways[c - 1] for c > 0. ways[c] carries the value from the row above. Return the last entry.
solutions.pseudocode:
ways = [start open ? 1 : 0, 0, ...]
for each row: for c: if shelf: ways[c] = 0 elif c > 0: ways[c] = (ways[c] + ways[c-1]) mod M
return ways[cols - 1]
commonMistakes: Resetting ways at the start of each row, which loses the 'from above' contribution.
Not zeroing shelf cells, which lets routes pass through them.
solutions.interviewExplanation: Routes into a cell come from above or from the left, so I count with a table. I keep a single row. Before an update, ways[c] is the value from the row above, and ways[c - 1] is already this row's left neighbor. Shelves reset to zero. That's O(rows × cols) time and O(cols) space, taking the modulo as I go.

steps.title: Step 2
steps.content: Row 1 '.#.': ways[0] stays 1, the shelf gives 0, ways[2] = 1 + 0 = 1, so ways = [1,0,1].
